text: Eject and Ejective [Lat. eiectum , from eiicere , to throw out]: Ger. Ejekt ; Fr. éject ; Ital. ejettivo (ejective). Some one else thought of in terms of the thinker's own consciousness of himself. In its earlier stages it amounts to the interpretation of external phenomena, expressions, signs, &c., as involving experience analogous to that of the percipient or thinker. Suggested by Clifford ( Seeing and Thinking ); employed by Romanes ( Matter , Mind , and Monism ), by whom the principle of ANTHROPOMORPHISM (q.v.) in theism is said to produce the 'world-eject'; by Morselli ( Semej . malat . ment ., ii) in pathological conditions; and by Baldwin ( Social and Eth . Interpret .), who makes the process of ejection a necessary and continuous factor in the development of the consciousness of PERSONALITY (q.v.). The adjective 'ejective' qualifies the matter or content which in a particular case constitutes the 'eject.' See also PERSONIFICATION. ( J.M.B. - G.F.S. )
